question: What is the difference between Salafi and Ash'ari theology?
answer:
This question is actually a very common one. Anybody who is in any way, fashion or form linked with the da'wah scene, or with the online debates and issues, or even with Islamic scholarship, they're very well aware of these two strands within mainstream Sunnism. At the same time, those that are not involved with the online da'wah scene, those that are not involved with Islamic academics, they are blissfully, alhamdulillah, unaware, and these two names might not even be known to them.

And so we have to really take a step back and understand that in the religion of Islam, of course, since the very beginning, since the death of the Prophet ﷺ, the Muslim community has attempted to interpret various issues and controversies in different ways. We are all aware of the Sunni-Shi'a divide, which again goes back to very, very early Islam. What a lot of people are vaguely aware of is that even within Ahl al-Sunnah, or Sunnism, there are a number of interpretations or trends. And these two terms that are being asked about today, they apply to two different interpretations, or two slightly different theologies, within mainstream Sunnism.

Now, of course, the term Sunni, and I've talked about this in other lectures, the term Sunni comes from Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah. This is a term that first was in vogue, we can say definitely, within the first 50 years of the death of the Prophet ﷺ. Within the first 100 years, we actually have references of treatises and people talking about Ahl al-Sunnah. So it's a very early term.

And the meaning of Ahl al-Sunnah, or Sunni, was the group of Muslims who were combined by a number of things. First and foremost, they viewed the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ as being of paramount importance, second only to the Qur'an. So this group of Muslims followed the Qur'an and the Sunnah; hence they're called Sunni. Now, of course, there are other interpretations of Islam. The Shi'a community considers the need to have a living imam. And so what the Sunnah does for the Sunnis, the imam does for the Shi'a community: he interprets the law. And so they have a different notion. And of course other groups have other interpretations of what they're going to follow. So the Sunni community wanted to follow the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ; hence they're called Ahl al-Sunnah.

Also, another thing that united all of them is the respect for the Sahabah. All of the Sahabah are considered to be worthy of respect, and the Sunni community does not say anything negative or bad about any Muslim who accompanied the Prophet ﷺ. That's another hallmark of Sunni Islam. Another hallmark of Sunni Islam is their belief in predestination, or Qadr. Non-Sunni groups generally do not believe in Qadr. They don't believe that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala wills the actions of the people, but rather that they have ultimate free will. And Ahl al-Sunnah believes that Allah knows, and also to a certain level wills as well, and therefore there is the belief in Qadr. And there are other aspects of Sunni Islam.

Now, this is generic Sunnism. By the way, one more thing we can say is that, historically speaking, the Sunni community gathered around the legitimate khalifah, whether it was the Umayyads or the Abbasids or the Ottomans or whoever their local governors were. Even if they didn't like them, they felt that the community is more important than breaking away and fighting against the caliph and whatnot. That's a legitimate khalifah, obviously, that used to exist in the past. Now, these are all things that combined mainstream, if you like, Sunnism.

Now, obviously, as time developed, within this strand, within this interpretation, various theologians came, and the finer details, or the more difficult questions, were answered in diverse manners. And therefore the question that I'm answering today: the two terms Salafi and Ash'ari. And to point out that both of these two terms are somewhat contested, in particular the term Salafism. The term Salafism applies to a strand or a group that actually has multiple terms: whether you call it Athari, or you call it Hanbali theology, or the modern iteration is Salafism, that is one strand. And it is considered to be the one that is predominant in Saudi Arabia and in other places in the Muslim world.

And the other strand we're talking about is Ash'arism. And that goes back to a particular individual by the name of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who died around 320 Hijrah. He was one of the first to develop a type of systematic theology that then paved the way for what we now call Ash'arism. And of course, in our times, we have very famous adherents to both of these strands. They go back very early in Islam. They have produced scholarship, they have produced ulama, they have produced works, they have produced institutions, and they are in some ways rival schools. They are rivaling one another, and they are competing for more adherents, and refutations, which is what happens when you have anything of this nature.

Now, how and why do they differ? And again, this is a very packed summary. Obviously, as usual, I give the caveat that so much more can be said; time is always limited. For those who are completely not aware of these differences, let me be very simplistic and summarize the differences in three primary ways, or three primary notions. This is not exhaustive; it's just an introduction.

First and foremost is the concept and the definition of iman. What exactly is iman? The Ash'ari movement, or the Ash'ari strand, says that iman is tasdiq, which is affirmation of the heart, or belief in the heart. So if you believe, then you are a Muslim and a mu'min. If you believe, then you have iman. Iman is that which is in the heart. It is to affirm with your heart, to know in your heart that Allah exists, the Prophet is true, the Qur'an is the book of Allah. If you know it in your heart and you believe it in your heart, then this is iman. So they say iman is tasdiq.

In contrast to this, the Athari school, or the Salafi school, says that iman is that which exists in the heart, is affirmed by the tongue, and is then practiced by the actions. And it goes up and it goes down; it increases and it decreases. Of course, the Ash'ari school believes that iman itself does not increase or decrease, because they view iman, and the analogy given is like a light switch, as binary: either one or zero. You either have it or you don't. It's either up, the light is on, or down, the light is off. So from their perspective, iman is very much like a binary code. You either have it or you don't. You either know Allah is true and your Creator, and the Prophet ﷺ is true, or you don't. There is no middle ground, and there is no increase or decrease of actual iman.

Whereas the Salafi school would say that iman, the actual term iman, consists of belief in the heart, statements of the tongue and actions of the limbs, and it increases and it decreases. It increases if you do more good deeds, or you're in a spiritual state of mind, you go for Hajj and Umrah, you're in the month of Ramadan; and it decreases when you're committing sins, when you're away from Allah 'azza wa jall, when your heart has ghaflah. And the actual term iman applies to actions as well. So actions, according to the Salafis, are an integral part of iman. It's not just a by-product; it is within the term iman, and what we call iman, it comes within it. And of course they therefore believe that actual iman increases and decreases. And therefore, when Allah says in the Qur'an that iman goes up:

> وَيَزْدَادَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِيمَانًا ... فَزَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا

that it's actually iman increasing and decreasing. As for the Ash'ari school, they interpret these verses to mean that their iman is affirmed, not necessarily that it increases. So this is one difference: the concept and definition of iman.

Another difference between the Salafi and Ash'ari schools is the importance and the methodology of proving the existence of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Generally speaking, the Ash'ari school, their textbooks of theology follow a particular methodology of beginning with trying to prove the existence of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and then doing that in a very particular method. It is called in English the kalam cosmological argument. This is a very specific method of proving Allah's existence. If you study any course about proving God's existence, if you study any book, you will find three or five or 10 or 15 different methods that have been used historically to try to prove the existence of Allah, or the existence of God. And one of them is called the kalam, or the cosmological proof, or the kalam cosmological proof.

And this is a proof that, in its very origins, goes back to Aristotle. You find reference to it actually even in Plato, you find a line or two, but Aristotle definitely has the rudimentary developments. But then early Muslim theologians from another school called Mu'tazilism, Abu al-Hudhayl al-'Allaf is one of the main people, they developed a very rudimentary methodology of proving Allah's existence. And this tactic, or this methodology, is then adopted by the Ash'ari school, and then sanitized, and then it becomes a feature of that school. Again, a very interesting way of doing that, beyond the scope of our particular Q&A here.

But basically, to be very, very simplistic, it relies on the fact that the world around us consists of actual bodies. So this is a body, the table is a body, I'm a body, everything is a body. And bodies have within them, subsisting within them, things that they call attributes, or accidents. And accidents are that which subsists within a body. And so an accident would be color or temperature or size, X, Y and Z coordinates. These are all accidents. By accidents we don't mean like a car accident; by accidents we mean that which subsists within a physical structure called a body. And so they have a very elaborate proof where they demonstrate that accidents must be created. And if accidents are created, and accidents can only exist in bodies, then bodies must also be created. And therefore, if the body is created, there must be a Creator who created the bodies. It's a very simplistic version of the kalam cosmological argument. And this is a backbone of Ash'ari theology: the existence of God is important to prove, and then how you prove it.

In contrast to this, the Salafi movement, generally speaking, says that the existence of God is something that does not require elaborate proofs, that it is something that is inherently ingrained in mankind, and that to deny this is to deny something that is self-evident. Hence, no matter how many proofs you try to give, it's somewhat of a waste of time. It's somewhat superfluous to try to prove the obvious. And so, generally speaking, the Salafi school does not prioritize philosophical proofs for the existence of God, believing that the existence of God is self-evident and does not require elaborate proofs.

And then, in particular, they say this mechanism of proving God is something that is, from their perspective, problematic. They say that this kalam cosmological argument, when it is employed, actually leads to subsidiaries or corollaries that are problematic. And most important is how this proof affects the interpretation of Allah's names and attributes, which is point number three of our list.

So point number one was the definition of iman. Point number two would be the importance of, and how one proves, the existence of God. The importance of proving: not the importance of believing, we all believe it's important to believe Allah exists, but the importance of proving that Allah exists. The Ash'ari school says the most important obligation is to prove Allah exists, and the Salafi school says the most important obligation is the worship of Allah. We assume, everybody should assume, that people know that Allah 'azza wa jall exists.

And then the third point of difference is the concept of Allah's attributes. And this is the most contentious, and this is what the schools are most famous for arguing about. This is really the area of controversy that any average internet user is aware of. Any average person who is involved with polemics, involved with online debates, involved with the various Muslim communities out there, they are well aware that this is the issue in which there's so much, sometimes even online, antagonism.

How does one understand the attributes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala? When Allah 'azza wa jall says, "The face of your Lord shall remain." When Allah says in the Qur'an that "I created Adam with both of My hands." When Allah says in the Qur'an, "The Rahman has risen over the throne." When Allah says in the Qur'an, "Your Lord will come on the Day of Judgment, and the angels will come rank upon rank." When the Prophet ﷺ said, "Our Lord comes down in the last third of the night." When Allah 'azza wa jall says, "They fear their Lord who is above them." How does one understand all of this genre of attributes?

As for the Salafi school, the Salafi school says that if Allah says it, Allah knows best how He is. And therefore we should simply affirm the word and not think about how. We don't think and we don't consider how. And so we leave the howness to Allah 'azza wa jall. If Allah 'azza wa jall says He has a wajh, a face, then we say He has a face, but we don't think about how it is. If Allah says He rises over the throne, so be it. This means He has a throne and He has risen over it, and we leave it at that; we don't think about how. This is called balkafah, or bila kayf: you negate the howness.

So the Salafi school is famous as the only school in all of Islam that affirmed every single verb or adjective or noun ascribed to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And they said the word's meaning is understood; the word's howness is relegated to Allah. We don't think how it is. So this is the Salafi paradigm.

As for the Ash'ari school, they said that we will only take seven of those attributes and affirm them with the bila kayf doctrine. So seven attributes we will affirm like the Salafis do, meaning, not exactly like, but let me just say for the purposes of our Q&A, that they will affirm them without any kayf, without how. And these are life and knowledge and will and power and hearing and seeing and speech. These are the seven attributes. The Ash'aris say Allah has life, hayah; and Allah has sam', and Allah has basar, and Allah has qudrah; and Allah 'azza wa jall is Sami' and Basir; and Allah has the sifah of kalam, and qudrah. So all of these we shall affirm, bila kayf; we're not going to think about how.

However, all the other attributes we cannot affirm, because that would imply that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has a body. And so this goes back to our kalam cosmological argument. One of the attributes is that of motion. Something moves; this is an attribute. Motion does not exist by itself; there must be a body that motion exists within. And so in order to prove point number two, which is how God exists, they have an elaborate proof, the kalam cosmological argument, and they prove that attributes are created, they prove that attributes must exist within bodies, and then they prove that bodies must be created. And one of the attributes is motion.

Now you come to the verse that your Lord has risen over the throne, and to rise is a type of motion. You come to the hadith, your Lord comes down, and that is a type of motion. You come to the verse of the Qur'an, "Your Lord comes," and that is a type of motion. And so the Ash'ari school says clearly Allah did not intend these literal meanings, because, they say, if you affirm those verbs, you are affirming the attribute of motion. And if you affirm the attribute of motion, this implies, a'udhu billah, that God is a body. And if God is a body, then, a'udhu billah, all bodies are created. Again, go back to the kalam cosmological proof: motion is an accident, accidents must exist in bodies, bodies are created. So if you ascribe to Allah istiwa' and nuzul and maji', if you ascribe to Allah these concepts, from the Ash'ari paradigm you will logically conclude that whoever has that attribute must also be, a'udhu billah, created. And so from their paradigm, they say, no, we cannot affirm those types of attributes to Allah.

And they also say the attributes of hand and face, this is anthropomorphic; it is human-like. And Allah says in the Qur'an, "There is nothing like Him." And so we say that all of this is metaphorical or symbolic. Or they might say, all of this, our minds should go blank, and we should not even think about the meaning of the word. Even the word, we just go blank. So when Allah says wajh, or face, we don't even think of wajh; we just go blank. That's one way of doing this; it's called tafwid. Or the other way is to say that, well, by face Allah meant His blessings, His countenance. By rising over the throne, Allah meant His dominion has conquered the world. And so it's called ta'wil, or reinterpretation.

So the Ash'ari school has two positions, both of which are fine for them. Position A: you completely block out any meaning, any linguistic meaning. As for the Salafi school, remember, they will say we'll affirm the linguistic meaning, but we will deny how it exists in Allah. We will say that Allah rises over the throne, but we won't think about how that occurs. And as for the Ash'ari school, they will say, no, clearly there is no actual throne, there is no actual rising over, and so it has to be negated. Then you have one of two options. Either you say, this whole phrase and passage, we simply go blank and don't think about it at all. Or it becomes metaphorical for: Allah has power over the entire creation. "Allah has risen over the throne": Allah has dominion over the entire creation.

So these are some of the main differences. And of course, one of the more common questions in the Salafi-Ash'ari debate online is the famous debate: where is Allah? Where is Allah? And the Salafi says that the Qur'an and Sunnah indicate that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is above us, and there are hundreds of verses and ahadith that indicate what is called transcendence, or that Allah is above: "That they fear the Lord who is above them." And the Prophet asked the slave girl, "Where is Allah?" and she said, "Allah is above us." And so there are so many ahadith and ayat. And then, to counter this, the Ash'ari school says you clearly don't mean above in the three-dimensional sense, because what is above for one part of the world is below for the other part, and because of three dimensions, and all of this goes on and on and on.

And by the way, this is a very brief intro. Every single point that I have said, the other group has a counterpoint, and the other group has a second counterpoint, and the other group has a third counterpoint, ad infinitum. It goes on and on and on. These debates have occupied the minds of theologians for, no exaggeration, 12, if not 13 centuries. And so much has been written. You could spend many lifetimes, no exaggeration, going deep into these controversies, back and forth and back and forth. And I would know, because this is my area of expertise, and I have in fact spent, not lifetimes, but many decades studying advanced issues of theology. So there is a lot to be said. We're summarizing here that these are some of the main differences between these two schools, the Salafi school and the Ash'ari school.

And of course these schools have famous scholars from the beginning of time. The Salafi school claims the likes of Imam Ahmad; of course, the most famous icon is Ibn Taymiyyah, and Ibn al-Qayyim. And the Ash'ari school has many famous ulama; their most famous icon is Imam al-Ghazali, for example. So you have various personalities throughout history who have manifested in both of these schools.

And to compound the problem, to make it even more complicated: all that I described to you is actually early, or classical, Salafism and Ash'arism. Historically, a lot of other things happened, because it's been around for 12 centuries, no exaggeration, 12 centuries. These two trends have existed side by side, at times moments of tension, at times moments of reconciliation. And so a lot has happened. And of the things that have happened, for reasons beyond the scope of our brief Q&A, is that the Salafi school has been associated with one particular madhhab, the Hanbali madhhab. Generally speaking, the Hanbali scholars were in some fashion or form within the spectrum of Salafism, or Atharism to be more precise, or Ahl al-Hadith as it is also called. And the Maliki and the Shafi'i schools gravitated towards Ash'arism.

By the way, a footnote here: there's a third trend as well. There's something called Maturidi, or Maturidism. So we have Ash'arism, Salafism and Maturidism. And Maturidis and Ash'aris are very, very close. The differences are even more abstract than what I've just done between Salafis and Ash'aris. For example, the Maturidis affirm eight attributes instead of seven: very, very small, very technical details between the Maturidi and the Ash'ari school. In reality, they even consider each other to be sister schools, and there's very little difference between them. And the Maturidi school was basically co-opted by the Hanafi madhhab. The Ottomans took the Hanafi school and the Maturidi school of theology and merged them together. And so historically, two of the madhhabs (in the beginning they had... but that's beyond the scope) became Ash'ari, one of them became Maturidi, and one of them became Salafi. And so that's been the reality for the last so many centuries.

And along with this, other changes came along which further complicated the discussions between them, which did not exist in the early founding of these schools. And of them, in particular, are various understandings of tasawwuf, of how one practices Sufism. And this is another major controversy between all of these schools. So, for example, to give you one simple example, and I'm not going to answer it here, but I'll just give it to you now: the Indians and Pakistanis are aware of the Barelvi movement and the Deobandi movement. Both Barelvis and Deobandis are under the Maturidi Hanafi spectrum. So you see now that you have a mother school, and that has two children, and then they divide too. It becomes more and more, and you have all of these splinters happening.

We haven't even begun the political divisions now, between political Islam and apolitical Islam, because that too plays a role in all of this type of interpretation. And then you have, of course, the understanding of tasawwuf and awliya, and the visitation of graves, and the veneration of graves, and the exaltation of saints, and the role of saints. All of this has permeated, so that the differences are no longer just those three, even though technically those three and some others should be the only differences. But historically, other differences were added. So, for example, to celebrate the Mawlid or to not celebrate the Mawlid: this is a classic divide between modern Salafism and modern Ash'arism. This did not exist 500 or 1,000 years ago; that division did not exist over Mawlid stuff. This is something that is, in the grand scale of things, relatively more recent.

In any case, I can go on and on and on, but you wanted a brief explanation, and this is a brief explanation. As I explained, you have very many ulama from the Salafi school, historically and in our times, and the University of Medina, which I graduated from, is associated with that strand of Islam as well. And it is predominant in Arabia, Saudi Arabia, and among the scholars that have studied there and have been influenced by the revivalistic movement of that region. And al-Azhar University, for example, is on the Ash'ari strand, and there are again many famous ulama, historically and in our times as well.

Now, these are some of the differences. Let us not forget, though, that the similarities between these two schools are actually far more than their differences, especially when you compare them to other strands of Islam. At the end of the day, both of these schools believe in the six pillars of iman as expressed in the Hadith of Jibril. Both of these schools affirm the Qur'an and the Sunnah as the primary sources of theology and law. Both of these schools have the same ways of looking at fiqh and of deriving fiqh. In fact, they have the same books of fiqh and the same scholars of fiqh, in the University of Medina and in al-Azhar. They studied the same curriculums in terms of the books of fiqh, the books of hadith, the books of usul al-fiqh, the books of history, the books of language, the books of tafsir. In reality, the scholars of each movement are studied by the scholars of the other, even if there are some tensions at times between modern understandings.

And that's something that needs to be stressed: what they share is far, far more than what they differ over. And historically, Salafis and Ash'aris have never divided themselves into different masajid, or into completely different... boycotting. I mean, unfortunately, sometimes you get calls to do that, but realistically, it's never happened, alhamdulillah, thumma alhamdulillah. And we need to keep it that way. The tensions, even though they should not be there, have always been at an academic level.

And my advice, as I conclude this question: in both of these strands, you have scholars that are aiming to exacerbate the tension. They want to make it worse. They want to preach against the other, and make the other into a deviant, and show how evil and misguided the other side is. And you also have scholars that try to work together and find commonality. And the fact of the matter, whether people like me saying this or not, is that the average Muslim is completely in blissful unawareness of these differences between these two strands. In fact, the differences between them do not affect the lay Muslim at all. They don't really translate to their daily life, in terms of these abstract issues of classical early Salafism and early Ash'arism.

And currently we are facing crises in every single arena of our life: political, economic, the nation-state issues, the various invasions taking place, the crises of Syria and of Afghanistan and of Palestine. On top of this, we have crises of intellectual challenges, and people are refuting aspects of our creed that we all agree upon. So rather than allow these tensions to increase, what we need to do is to work to minimize, in fact, to eradicate any tensions. Now, I am not saying that these differences are trivial. What I am saying is that we should not make a big deal out of them.

And those who want to dedicate their lives to the study of Islam, at some point they will have to make a choice: which textbooks they want to study, and which groups of scholars they want to study with. I myself had to make the choice 20, what, 25 years ago. I chose between Medina and Azhar, for example. I went the way that I did; I do not regret that. So at some point you might have to make that choice. But if you make such a choice to study with one side, don't demonize the other side. Don't consider the other side to be, a'udhu billah, evil or misguided or going to Jahannam, a'udhu billah. There is iman and taqwa across all sides, and there's also nifaq and fisq on all sides as well. You have genuine piety and you have the opposite.

So just because you study one version of Islam versus the other does not make you more pious. We have to be very clear about this. Piety transcends these human creeds and these differences between us. And you find righteous ulama and righteous 'ubbad and awliya in both of these strands, and in fact in more than just these two strands. And we need to look at that as well. So what we have in common is far, far more important than what divides us.

And therefore we should not give platforms to preachers who exacerbate tensions between these movements. Rather, we should simply not even pay them attention, because there are people like this on both sides, by the way. And I'll be honest here: 25 years ago, I myself was more sympathetic to that strand of harshness, and considering that to be deviant. But that's young age, when I was 20; it's different now. Wisdom and experience teach you; seeing the realities of the ummah reorients your mind here. SubhanAllah, these are people, both sides, that are praying to the same God, following the same fiqh even, the same methodology to pray even. Not even differences in fiqh and usul al-fiqh; they're pretty much the same in everything. It's just certain abstract notions that... in any case.

So my point being, you asked a question; this is the answer to it. I summarized the differences. And I say that Salafism and Ash'arism, and you can add Maturidism as well, are two or three sister strands within mainstream Sunnism, and there are differences, and let the advanced students study those differences. **But the average person should never, ever make those differences the defining characteristic of himself or of the other.** And the laity of the ummah, really, alhamdulillah, there's no need for them to really get involved in these labels whatsoever, because it does not affect them in their daily lives. And alhamdulillah, thumma alhamdulillah, what unites these two strands is so much more that really we can say that, for practical purposes, the differences are really trivial. And that's the way that we should look at these two strands. And in the end, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
